findings.user_visible_behavior: Trusted-proxy honor: an untrusted caller's X-Forwarded-For header MUST be IGNORED so an attacker cannot forge their source IP and dodge the per-IP rate-limit backoff (§6.J spirit, documented in the function's own doc-comment).
findings.mutation: Replaced the `for _, n := range trusted { if n.Contains(rIP) { ... } }` guard with an unconditional `xff := c.GetHeader("X-Forwarded-For"); if xff != "" { return first }` — i.e. honor XFF from EVERY caller regardless of trusted-proxy CIDR membership (the canonical IP-spoofing bypass).

findings.action: none — existing test discriminates the security bypass correctly

findings.user_visible_behavior: A tracker password that legitimately CONTAINS a colon (e.g. 'p@ss:w0rd:!') MUST be forwarded whole to the upstream tracker. The parser uses strings.SplitN(credValue, ":", 2) so the username is parts[0] and the ENTIRE remainder is the password.
findings.observed_pre_gap_close: ok — MUTATION SURVIVED. Existing TestParseAuthToken_PasswordFormat uses 'myuser:mypass' (no colon in password), so len(pwParts)==2 still holds; the colon-bearing-password regression is invisible. A user whose password contains ':' would get zero-value Credentials (username+password both unset) and FAIL to authenticate against kinozal/nnmclub — uncaught.
findings.action: Added TestParseAuthToken_PasswordWithColonPreserved in internal/auth/multiprovider_test.go asserting username='alice' AND password='p@ss:w0rd:!' (two colons) are both preserved.
